title: Botanical Extracts and Antagonistic Fungi for the Sustainable Management of Wheat Blast Caused by Pyricularia oryzae Triticum Pathotype
content: Wheat blast, caused by Pyricularia oryzae Triticum pathotype (PoT), is a major threat to wheat production and highlights the need for sustainable alternatives to conventional fungicides. This study evaluated the antifungal, plant growth-promoting, and disease-suppressive effects of botanical extracts from Lippia alba and Allium sativum and the antagonistic fungi Trichoderma harzianum and Epicoccum nigrum against PoT under in vitro and in vivo conditions. In dual-culture and poisoned-food assays, A. sativum extract (867 ppm diallyl disulfide equivalent) and T. harzianum (TH-FCCT-1155-4) strongly inhibited PoT, completely suppressing conidiation and reducing mycelial growth by more than 90% and 58%, respectively. Seed treatments with A. sativum, T. harzianum, and E. nigrum were non-phytotoxic and significantly enhanced several seedling growth parameters, including leaf emission, stem thickness, and dry biomass, while reducing seed-to-seedling disease transmission. Foliar applications at the seedling (GS 1.5) and anthesis (GS 6.0) stages reduced disease development, as evidenced by lower AUDPC and spike severity. Disease severity remained below 30–40% in treated plants compared with more than 80% in untreated controls, while thousand-kernel weight and grain yield were not significantly reduced across susceptible wheat cultivars. In contrast, L. alba showed phytotoxic effects at 1000 ppm and increased spike severity associated with the solvent when applied at anthesis. RT-qPCR analysis further showed that A. sativum seed treatment modulated selected host defense responses in susceptible wheat, significantly upregulating PR5 and APX expression at 48–72 h post-inoculation. Overall, the results identify A. sativum, T. harzianum, and E. nigrum as promising biological and botanical tools for the integrated management of wheat blast and provide evidence that their protective effects may involve direct antifungal activity and, in the case of A. sativum, modulation of host defense responses.
